title: Marked interval nerve top-diagonal deletion is anodyne
statement: Use ordinary nerves and standard simplices of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones] and marked simplicial sets and the marked-anodyne class of [lem-coef-marked-anodyne-lifting-calculus]. For an integer $n\geq1$, let $T_n$ be the finite poset of pairs $(i,j)$ with $0\leq i\leq j\leq n$, ordered by $(i,j)\leq(i',j')$ if $i\leq i'\leq j'\leq j$. For a proper subset $F\subsetneq\{0,\ldots,n\}$, let $T_F$ be the full subposet with both coordinates in $F$, and let $B_n\subseteq N(T_n)$ be the union of all $N(T_F)$. Let $Q_n\subseteq T_n$ be the full subposet obtained by deleting $(n,n)$, put $Y_n=N(Q_n)$, and put $D_n=B_n\cap Y_n$. Mark an edge in $Y_n$ exactly when its first coordinate is constant, and give $D_n$ the induced marking; in particular all degenerate edges are marked. Then the marked inclusion $D_n\hookrightarrow Y_n$ is marked anodyne.

source.place: Agent combinatorial auxiliary for the finite-simplex terminal comparison in proof paragraph 2; the marked-anodyne class is HTT Definition 3.1.1.1. This particular interval-poset assertion is not attributed to HTT or to Cisinski, and has no Stacks tag.

proof.text: By the nerve convention in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], nondegenerate simplices are strict chains of intervals. Define their support to be the union of their endpoint coordinates. Membership in $D_n$ is exactly proper support, since a chain belongs to $N(T_F)$ precisely when all endpoints belong to $F$. A full-support chain starts at $(0,n)$: if its initial left endpoint were positive, $0$ could never occur; if its initial right endpoint were less than $n$, $n$ could never occur. Between successive $(i,j),(k,l)$ one has $k-i\leq1$ and $j-l\leq1$: an integer strictly between $i$ and $k$ could occur neither as a left endpoint (the left endpoints skip it) nor as a right endpoint (all right endpoints before the jump are at least $k$, and afterwards at least the current left endpoint). The right-endpoint argument is symmetric. The final width is at most one, since an integer strictly between the final endpoints never occurred. Consequently the chain is a path starting at $(0,n)$, using steps $H:(i,j)\mapsto(i,j-1)$, $V:(i,j)\mapsto(i+1,j)$ or $D:(i,j)\mapsto(i+1,j-1)$, and ending at width zero or one, without $(n,n)$. Conversely every such path has full support: the successive endpoints cover the integers from both ends inward, with no integer left strictly between the final endpoints.

source.place: Agent combinatorial auxiliary for the finite-simplex terminal comparison; support and exact path description.

proof.text: Here is a total rule $P$ on full-support chains. Scan the path word from the beginning for the first occurrence of either a letter $D$ or two consecutive letters $HV$ (compare their starting positions). At a $D$ starting at $(i,j)$, insert $(i,j-1)$, replacing $D$ by $HV$. At an $HV$ starting at $(i,j)$, delete its middle vertex $(i,j-1)$, replacing $HV$ by $D$. If neither occurs, the word is $V^aH^b$. When its final width is one, append the vertex $(i,i)$ to its final vertex $(i,i+1)$, i.e. append $H$. When its final width is zero, delete the final $H$ and its target vertex. This last $H$ exists: otherwise the path would be all $V$ and end at the forbidden $(n,n)$. All insertions remain in $Q_n$: the inserted vertex at a $D$ has $i<j-1$, and the appended $(i,i)$ has $i<n$. All deletions retain full support by the path description. Thus there is no unspecified fallback branch or choice of an available face.

source.place: Agent combinatorial auxiliary for the finite-simplex terminal comparison; explicit horizontal-priority matching, including end cases.

proof.text: The rule is an involution. Replacing the first $D$ by $HV$ creates no earlier $D$ or $HV$: the prefix is unchanged and its last letter followed by the new $H$ cannot form $HV$. Hence the new first feature is exactly the inserted $HV$; deletion reverses the insertion. Replacing a first $HV$ by $D$ similarly creates no earlier feature, and insertion reverses it. In the feature-free end cases, appending or deleting the final $H$ leaves a word $V^aH^b$, with no $D$ or $HV$, and switches final width one and zero. These end operations are inverse as well. Every full-support chain therefore belongs to exactly one pair $(\sigma,\tau)$, where $\tau$ has one more vertex and $\sigma$ is obtained by deleting the chosen vertex of $\tau$. In particular the rule covers all missing simplices, rather than merely counting them. Call $\tau$ the upper chain of the pair and $\sigma$ its lower chain.

source.place: Agent combinatorial auxiliary for the finite-simplex terminal comparison; involutivity, uniqueness and coverage of the matching.

proof.text: Order the pairs by the key $(\dim\tau,\tau)$, increasing, where the second component is the lexicographic list of vertices and vertices are ordered lexicographically by $(i,j)$ with $i$ first. This is an explicit finite order. We check that every codimension-one face $f$ of $\tau$, other than $\sigma$, either has proper support or belongs to a strictly earlier pair. For a full-support interior deletion, the two merged steps must be $HV$ or $VH$: $HH$ skips a right endpoint, $VV$ skips a left endpoint, and any combination involving $D$ skips at least one endpoint. Deleting the first vertex loses $0$ or $n$. Deleting the last vertex can have full support only if $\tau$ ends on a diagonal and its last step is $H$ or $V$; its final width then becomes one. If $f$ is itself an upper chain its pair has upper dimension $\dim\tau-1$, hence is earlier. It remains to check the cases where $f$ is lower, done next.

source.place: Agent combinatorial auxiliary for the finite-simplex terminal comparison; finite attachment order and classification of all full-support facets.

proof.text: Suppose first that $\tau$ has a selected first $HV$. Deleting the middle vertex of any later $HV$ preserves the selected feature, so the face is upper. Deleting the middle vertex of a $VH$ creates a $D$. If this $VH$ precedes the selected $HV$, or overlaps it in the last two letters of $HVH$, the face is lower: its partner replaces that $VH$ by $HV$. Otherwise the selected $HV$ survives and the face is upper. In each lower case the partner agrees with $\tau$ until the changed corner, where its vertex $(i,j-1)$ replaces $(i+1,j)$, strictly decreasing the vertex list. For a full-support last-vertex deletion, the face is upper if the selected $HV$ survives. The only remaining case is that the word ends in the selected $HV$; deleting its final $V$ target leaves a feature-free word of final width one. Its partner appends $H$ instead, again replacing $(i+1,j)$ by $(i,j-1)$ and decreasing the list. Suppose instead that $\tau$ has no $D$ or $HV$. It ends on a diagonal with word $V^aH^b$, $b>0$. Its last-vertex deletion is its partner $\sigma$; every other full-support facet deletes the sole possible $VH$ corner and has partner obtained by changing $VH$ to $HV$, with the same strict lexicographic decrease. These exhaust the preceding facet classification. Thus in every case the pair containing $f\ne\sigma$ is earlier: its upper dimension drops, or is unchanged and its vertex list drops. This proves well-foundedness of the attachment dependencies, not merely a dimension change within each pair.

source.place: Agent combinatorial auxiliary for the finite-simplex terminal comparison; complete rank decrease for every other facet, hence acyclicity.

proof.text: Start with $D_n$ and process the pairs in that order. Inductively all faces of $\tau$ except $\sigma$ are present by the preceding rank check. Neither $\sigma$ nor $\tau$ has already appeared: initially both have full support, and each earlier attachment adds just its own two paired nondegenerate simplices, by this same induction. Write $d=\dim\tau$ and let $r$ be the deleted vertex index. Every proper face of $\sigma$ belongs to another codimension-one face of $\tau$, so it is already present. Thus the underlying intersection of $\Delta^d= N(\tau)$ with the old stage is exactly $\Lambda_r^d$, using the explicit horn definition in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. This also handles $d=1$, where the horn is the other vertex. In every degree, adjoining $\Delta^d$ along this intersection adds exactly $\sigma,\tau$ and their degeneracies; the nerve of a strict poset chain is an embedded standard simplex. Hence the stated induction is a filtration by simplicial subsets, with no requirement that a first insertion's other faces be available before its rank.

source.place: Agent combinatorial auxiliary for the finite-simplex terminal comparison; direct horn-intersection induction and underlying pushout.

proof.text: The chosen vertex is never the initial $(0,n)$, so $1\leq r\leq d$. In an interior pair it is the middle vertex of $HV$, so $0<r<d$. In an end pair it is the appended $H$ target, so $r=d$ and the final edge has constant first coordinate. Use respectively generators (i) and (ii) of [lem-coef-marked-anodyne-lifting-calculus]. For $d\geq3$ every edge of $\Delta^d$ belongs to the horn. All markings beyond those in the generator are therefore already present on the old stage: pushing out the generator along the horn map preserves them and creates exactly the induced marked simplex. For the final generator the required final edge is marked by the constant-first calculation. For $d=1$ only the final case occurs: $n=1$, $\tau=((0,1),(0,0))$, and generator (ii) adds its marked edge and missing source vertex.

source.place: Agent combinatorial auxiliary for the finite-simplex terminal comparison; horn index, exclusion of index zero, and markings in dimensions one and at least three.

proof.text: It remains to check the edge newly appearing when $d=2$. For an inner pair the word is $HV$, so the missing long edge has different first endpoints; it is unmarked, exactly as in generator (i). For a final pair the new edge is $[0,1]$, while $[1,2]$ is the marked final $H$ edge and $[0,2]$ belongs to the old horn. Apply generator (ii), adding the triangle and leaving $[0,1]$ unmarked. If the first coordinates of vertices $0,1$ differ, this is already the induced marking. If they agree, all three first coordinates agree, since $[1,2]$ is $H$. Therefore $[0,2]$ and $[1,2]$ are both marked. Push out [lem-coef-marked-triangle-cancellation] to mark $[0,1]$. Its class $W$ is the same marked-anodyne class: the four families and closure operations in its statement are exactly those in [lem-coef-marked-anodyne-lifting-calculus]. This is cancellation of the initial edge from the marked long and final edges, not generator (iii) for composition of consecutive marked edges. No nonconstant-first edge is marked by this operation.

source.place: Agent combinatorial auxiliary for the finite-simplex terminal comparison; dimension-two marking cases, using cancellation for the missing initial edge.

proof.text: At each stage give the old subcomplex the marking induced from $Y_n$. The preceding cases construct the next such stage by a pushout of generator (i) or (ii), followed, only when required, by a triangle-cancellation pushout. The underlying pushout is the degreewise union proved above; its marking is the union of the input marked edges, since a map out of this union preserves markings precisely when its two restrictions do. The same observation applies to the marking-only pushout. There are finitely many pairs, since $Q_n$ is a finite poset and has finitely many strict chains. The matching covers every full-support chain, and proper-support chains were present initially; the last stage is consequently $Y_n$ with exactly its required marking. Closure under pushouts and finite compositions, as stated in [lem-coef-marked-anodyne-lifting-calculus], proves that $D_n\hookrightarrow Y_n$ is marked anodyne. For $n=1$ this filtration is the single generator already identified; no dimension-zero attachment or extra hypothesis is used.

source.place: Agent combinatorial auxiliary for the finite-simplex terminal comparison; marked pushouts, exhaustion and global conclusion.

proof_origin.place: Agent combinatorial auxiliary; explicit H/V/D involutive matching, dimension-lexicographic attachment order, all horn intersections and induced markings.
